note: The periods of each composer of score-reader's catalogue: the second half of a narrow unit (a composer in one kind of piece and one period; the kind comes from score-reader's facts). A work falls in the first period whose years hold the year a source states for it (score-reader facts), else whose catalogue numbers or label hold it. A work no line holds belongs to no period, and its unit falls back to the composer. Written on 21 November 2026 from the usual divisions of each composer's life and works and the dates of composition the standard work lists give; a judgment table, each line with its reason. Numbers are ranges [first, last] or single numbers; 'except' takes numbers out of a range for another period, listed first. A composer with one period has no division that the catalogue's works would separate, or too few works to divide.

Ludwig van Beethoven.source: the three periods as drawn since Wilhelm von Lenz (1852): early to the Heiligenstadt crisis (1802), middle 1803 to 1814, late from 1815; opus numbers follow composition for the most part, the early works published late taken out by their dates of composition

periods.name: early
periods.why: to 1802; op. 65, 66, 71, 81b, 87, 103, 116 and 129 were written by 1802 and published later

periods.name: middle
periods.why: 1803 (the Eroica, the Waldstein, op. 53) to 1814; op. 113, 117, 118, 136 and 138 date from 1807 to 1814

periods.name: late
periods.why: from 1815 (op. 98, An die ferne Geliebte, 1816; the cello sonatas op. 102, 1815) to the last quartets

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.source: Köchel numbers follow the order of composition; the usual division by his years: childhood and youth, the Salzburg years from 1773, Vienna from 1781

periods.name: youth
periods.why: to 1773, the journeys of the child and the young man

periods.name: Vienna
periods.why: from Idomeneo, K. 366 (1780-81), to the Requiem

Franz Joseph Haydn.source: the usual division: the early works, the Sturm und Drang years (about 1766-1773), the mature works to 1790, then London and the late works; the quartets by opus, the symphonies by the groups whose dates are certain

periods.name: early
periods.why: the first quartets, op. 1 and op. 2 (1757-62)

periods.name: Sturm und Drang
periods.why: the quartets op. 9, 17 and 20 (1769-72) and the minor-key symphonies of those years

periods.name: mature
periods.why: the quartets from op. 33 (1781) to op. 64 (1790); the Paris symphonies and nos. 88-92

periods.name: London and late
periods.why: the London symphonies (1791-95) and the last quartets

Franz Schubert.source: Deutsch numbers follow the order of composition; the late works are usually counted from the Unfinished Symphony (D 759, 1822)

periods.name: before 1822
periods.why: the songs and works of his first ten years

Frédéric Chopin.source: Warsaw to 1830, Paris from 1831, and the late works from 1843; opus numbers follow publication, which for op. 1-65 follows composition closely; the posthumous op. 66-74 are mostly early

periods.name: Warsaw
periods.why: to his leaving Poland (1830): op. 1-14, the F minor concerto op. 21, and the posthumous op. 66-74, mostly written then

periods.name: late
periods.why: from the Nocturnes op. 55 (1843) to the Cello Sonata op. 65 and the last mazurkas

Johannes Brahms.source: opus numbers follow composition; the early works to 1860, the late works from the Clarinet Trio (1891)

periods.name: early
periods.why: the sonatas, the Ballades and the first concerto, to the First Sextet (op. 18, 1860)

periods.name: late
periods.why: the clarinet works, the piano pieces op. 116-119, the Four Serious Songs and the chorale preludes

Robert Schumann.source: the piano years to 1839, the song year 1840 and the years of symphony and chamber music to 1849, and Düsseldorf from 1850; opus numbers follow composition with the exceptions listed

periods.name: piano years
periods.why: the piano cycles, op. 1 to 23, with op. 26, 28 and 32 (1838-39)

periods.name: 1840 to 1849
periods.why: from the song year to 1849; op. 124 gathers pieces of 1832-45

Franz Liszt.source: the virtuoso years to 1847, Weimar 1848-1861, Rome and the late years from 1861; S numbers do not follow composition, so each work is placed by the year of the version the catalogue reads

periods.name: virtuoso years
periods.why: the Petrarch sonnets in their first version (S. 270a, 1842-46)
periods.label: S\.270a

periods.name: Weimar
periods.why: the final versions of the Transcendental and Paganini studies (1851), the Années Suisse and Italie as published (1855, 1858) and Venezia e Napoli (1859), the Second Ballade and the Sonata (1853), the Consolations (1849-50), the Hungarian Rhapsodies (1846-53), the First Mephisto Waltz (1859-61)

periods.name: late
periods.why: from 1862: the two concert studies (1862-63) and the second version of the Petrarch sonnets (S. 270b, revised in the 1860s, published 1883); a key S 270 alone does not say which version, so the version is read from the title
periods.label: S\.270b

Johann Sebastian Bach.source: Weimar 1708-1717, Köthen 1717-1723, Leipzig 1723-1750; BWV numbers follow kind, not date, so only the works whose place is certain are placed

periods.name: Köthen
periods.why: the Inventions and Sinfonias (1720-23), the first book of the Well-Tempered Clavier (1722), the solo violin and cello works (about 1720) and the Brandenburg Concertos (1721)

periods.name: Leipzig
periods.why: the four-part chorales (most from his Leipzig cantatas and Passions), the Partitas (1726-31), the second book of the Well-Tempered Clavier (1742), the Goldberg Variations (1741), the Musical Offering (1747) and the Art of Fugue

Claudio Monteverdi.source: Cremona and early Mantua (books 1-3, 1587-92), Mantua and the seconda pratica (books 4-5, 1603-05), Venice from 1613

periods.name: early
periods.label: (?i)primo libro|secondo libro|terzo libro
periods.why: the first three books of madrigals

periods.name: seconda pratica
periods.label: (?i)quarto libro|quinto libro
periods.why: the fourth and fifth books (1603, 1605), which Artusi attacked and Monteverdi defended

periods.name: Venice
periods.label: (?i)sesto libro|settimo libro|ottavo libro|guerrier|amoros|sestina|maddalena|\bSV 2(?:5[2-9]|[6-8][0-9])\b
periods.why: from the sixth book (1614, with the Sestina) to the eighth (1638), the Musiche per la Maddalena (1617) and the sacred works of the Selva morale (SV 252-288, 1641); the Vespers of 1610 (SV 206) are not placed

Arnold Schoenberg.source: tonal to 1908, free atonality 1908-1920, twelve-tone from 1921

periods.name: tonal
periods.why: to the Second String Quartet (op. 10, 1907-08), which ends beyond tonality

periods.name: atonal
periods.why: from the Three Piano Pieces op. 11 (1909)

periods.name: twelve-tone
periods.why: from the Five Piano Pieces op. 23 (1920-23)

Anton Webern.source: tonal works, free atonality, and the twelve-tone works from op. 17 (1924)

periods.name: tonal
periods.why: the Passacaglia op. 1 and the choral canon op. 2 (1908)

periods.name: atonal
periods.why: from the George songs op. 3 to the canons op. 16

Alban Berg.source: the tonal early works, free atonality from op. 3, the twelve-tone works from the Lyric Suite (1926)

periods.name: early
periods.why: the Piano Sonata and the songs op. 2

periods.name: atonal
periods.why: from the String Quartet op. 3 (1910) to Wozzeck

Alexander Scriabin.source: the early works in Chopin's line to op. 29, the middle works from the Fourth Sonata (op. 30, 1903), the late works from op. 58 (1910)

periods.name: middle
periods.why: from the Fourth Sonata (op. 30, 1903) to the Poem of Ecstasy's years

periods.name: late
periods.why: from op. 58 (1910) and Prometheus (op. 60) to the last preludes

periods.name: exile
periods.why: the six works written after he left Russia

Antonín Dvořák.source: the American years 1892-1895 are certain by opus; the opus numbers before them were assigned partly out of order by his publisher, so no earlier division is drawn by number

periods.name: before America
periods.why: before September 1892; the opus numbers of this range are not all in order, but all fall before America

periods.name: America
periods.why: from the New World Symphony (op. 95) to the Cello Concerto (op. 104)

periods.name: late
periods.why: after his return: the last quartets, the symphonic poems and the operas

Gabriel Fauré.source: the three periods usually drawn: to about 1885, 1885-1906, from 1906; by opus number only roughly

periods.name: middle
periods.why: from the Pavane (op. 50, 1887) and the Requiem's years to 1906

periods.name: late
periods.why: from La chanson d'Ève (op. 95, 1906-10) to the String Quartet

Claude Debussy.source: the early works to 1892, the mature works from the Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894), the late works from 1913; placed by the year a source states

periods.name: late
periods.why: the Études, the three sonatas and the late piano and stage works

George Frideric Handel.source: Hamburg and Italy to 1710, London from 1711; HWV numbers follow kind, not date

Richard Wagner.source: the romantic operas to Lohengrin (1848), the music dramas from Das Rheingold (1853-54); every work the catalogue holds is of the second

periods.name: romantic operas
periods.label: (?i)rienzi|holländer|hollander|tannhäuser|tannhauser|lohengrin
periods.why: Rienzi, Der fliegende Holländer, Tannhäuser, Lohengrin

periods.name: music dramas
periods.label: (?i)rheingold|walküre|siegfried|götterdämmerung|tristan|meistersinger|parsifal|wesendonck
periods.why: from Das Rheingold; the Wesendonck songs (1857-58) are studies for Tristan

Gustav Mahler.source: the Wunderhorn years to 1900, the Rückert years from 1901

periods.name: Wunderhorn years
periods.label: (?i)fahrenden gesellen|wunderhorn
periods.why: the Songs of a Wayfarer (1884-85) and the Wunderhorn songs (1887-1901)

periods.name: middle
periods.label: (?i)kindertotenlieder|rückert|ruckert
periods.why: the Kindertotenlieder (1901-04) and the Rückert songs (1901-02)

periods.name: late
periods.label: (?i)lied von der erde
periods.why: Das Lied von der Erde and the last symphonies

Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky.source: no division the catalogue's 28 works would separate usefully

Felix Mendelssohn.source: his style was formed by about 1825 and changed little; no usual division

Béla Bartók.source: 23 works; no division drawn by number here

Modest Mussorgsky.source: 17 works, most of them the numbers of Pictures at an Exhibition (1874)

Erik Satie.source: no division the catalogue's works would separate usefully

Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach.source: Berlin and Hamburg; Wq numbers follow kind, not date, and no year is stated for most

Domenico Scarlatti.source: Kirkpatrick's order follows the copying of the Venice and Parma manuscripts (1752-57), not composition

Antonio Vivaldi.source: RV numbers follow kind; the opus numbers are dates of publication

Arcangelo Corelli.source: six opus numbers, 1681-1714, each of one kind: the kind separates them

Jean-Philippe Rameau.source: 108 works, most of them numbers of the operas and the harpsichord books

John Dowland.source: the lute songs and lute pieces, 1597-1612

Thomas Tallis.source: the Latin works before the Reformation and the English works after it are separated by kind and language, not here

François Couperin.source: the harpsichord books (1713-1730) and the concerts (1722-24)

Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina.source: one period: his style is held to be one from the first book of Masses (1554) to his death (1594); CPDL dates most works only by their first printing, many after his death
